title: Basic Logic Gates (Gate Level)
description: Implement all basic logic gates using gate-level modeling. You must instantiate primitive gates to create: AND, OR, NAND, NOR, NOT (on input b), XOR, and XNOR gates. Use only Verilog gate primitives (and, or, nand, nor, not, xor, xnor). Do not use assign statements or behavioral modeling.
hint: Use: and gate1(output, input1, input2); not gate2(output, input); etc.

examples.output: and_out=0, or_out=1, nand_out=1, nor_out=0, notb_out=0, xor_out=1, xnor_out=0
examples.explanation: For inputs a=0, b=1: AND=0, OR=1, NAND=1, NOR=0, NOT(b)=0, XOR=1, XNOR=0

examples.output: and_out=1, or_out=1, nand_out=0, nor_out=0, notb_out=0, xor_out=0, xnor_out=1
examples.explanation: For inputs a=1, b=1: AND=1, OR=1, NAND=0, NOR=0, NOT(b)=0, XOR=0, XNOR=1

title: Basic Logic Gates (Dataflow)
description: Implement all basic logic gates using dataflow modeling with continuous assignment statements. Create: AND, OR, NAND, NOR, NOT (on input b), XOR, and XNOR gates. Use only assign statements with Verilog operators (&, |, ~&, ~|, ~, ^, ~^).
hint: Use: assign and_out = a & b; assign nand_out = ~(a & b); etc.

examples.output: and_out=0, or_out=1, nand_out=1, nor_out=0, notb_out=1, xor_out=1, xnor_out=0

title: Half Adder
description: Implement a half adder circuit. A half adder adds two single-bit binary numbers and produces a sum and carry output. The sum is calculated as XOR of inputs, and carry is calculated as AND of inputs. This is a fundamental building block for arithmetic circuits.
hint: Sum is XOR operation, carry is AND operation

title: Full Adder
description: Implement a full adder circuit. A full adder adds three single-bit binary numbers (two inputs and a carry-in) and produces a sum and carry-out. This is essential for multi-bit addition. The sum is XOR of all three inputs, and carry-out is majority function of inputs.
hint: Sum is three-way XOR, carry is OR of three AND terms

title: Full Adder using Half Adders
description: Implement a full adder by composing two half adders. This demonstrates hierarchical design in digital circuits. First half adder adds a and b, second half adder adds that result with cin, and final carry is OR of both half adder carries.
hint: Implement the logic of two half adders without actually instantiating them
constraints: Implement logic equivalent to two half adders

title: Half Subtractor
description: Implement a half subtractor circuit. A half subtractor subtracts two single-bit binary numbers and produces a difference and borrow output. The difference is XOR of inputs, and borrow is NOT(a) AND b. This is fundamental for subtraction circuits.
hint: Difference is XOR like half adder, but borrow logic is different

title: Full Subtractor
description: Implement a full subtractor circuit. A full subtractor subtracts three single-bit binary numbers (minuend a, subtrahend b, and borrow-in bin) and produces a difference and borrow-out. Essential for multi-bit subtraction. Difference is XOR of all inputs, borrow-out is more complex.
hint: Difference is three-way XOR like full adder, but borrow logic uses NOT(a)

title: Full Subtractor using Half Subtractors
description: Implement a full subtractor by composing two half subtractors. This demonstrates hierarchical design similar to full adder. First half subtractor calculates a-b, second calculates that result minus bin, and final borrow is OR of both half subtractor borrows.
hint: Implement logic of two half subtractors without instantiating them
constraints: Implement logic equivalent to two half subtractors

title: 4-bit Ripple Carry Adder
description: Implement a 4-bit ripple carry adder that adds two 4-bit numbers with a carry-in and produces a 4-bit sum and carry-out. This adder chains four 1-bit full adders together, where the carry-out of each stage becomes the carry-in of the next stage. This is a simple but slow adder design.
hint: Create intermediate carry signals between bits

title: 2-to-1 Multiplexer
description: Implement a 2-to-1 multiplexer (MUX). A multiplexer selects one of two input signals based on a select line. When select=0, output=input a; when select=1, output=input b. This is a fundamental data selection circuit used in many digital systems.
hint: Use conditional operator or Boolean algebra: out = (~s & a) | (s & b)

examples.explanation: Select line s=0 chooses input a=1
Select line s=1 chooses input b=0

title: 8-to-1 Multiplexer
description: Implement an 8-to-1 multiplexer that selects one of eight 1-bit inputs based on a 3-bit select signal. The output should be the input corresponding to the binary value of the select lines. This is commonly used in data routing and selection circuits.
hint: Use case statement or if-else ladder

examples.explanation: Select line 001 chooses in[1] which is 1
Select line 100 chooses in[4] which is 0

title: 1-to-8 Demultiplexer
description: Implement a 1-to-8 demultiplexer (DEMUX) with enable. A demultiplexer routes a single input to one of eight outputs based on a 3-bit select signal. When enable=1, the selected output gets the input value; all others get 0. When enable=0, all outputs are 0.
hint: Use case statement inside always block, set default to all zeros

examples.explanation: Input routed to output 2, others are 0

title: 8-to-3 Encoder
description: Implement an 8-to-3 binary encoder. An encoder converts 8 one-hot inputs into a 3-bit binary code. Only one input should be active at a time. The output is the binary representation of the active input index (0-7). Default output is 000 when no input is active.
hint: Use case statement with 8 cases for each input

title: Priority Encoder
description: Implement a 4-input priority encoder. A priority encoder gives priority to higher-index inputs. If multiple inputs are active, the output is the binary code of the highest priority active input. Input 3 has highest priority, input 0 has lowest.
hint: Use if-else or nested conditions checking from highest to lowest priority

examples.explanation: in[1] and in[0] both active, in[1] has higher priority
in[3] and in[2] both active, in[3] has highest priority

title: 4-bit Magnitude Comparator
description: Implement a 4-bit magnitude comparator that compares two 4-bit numbers A and B. The circuit produces three outputs: gt (A > B), eq (A == B), and lt (A < B). Only one output should be high at a time.
hint: Use >, ==, < operators directly
constraints: Only one output high at a time

title: Decimal to BCD Encoder
description: Implement a decimal to BCD (Binary Coded Decimal) encoder. Converts a 10-bit one-hot decimal input (0-9) to a 4-bit BCD output. Only one of the 10 inputs should be active at a time. Output is the 4-bit binary representation of the active decimal digit.
hint: Each output bit is OR of inputs where that bit should be 1 in BCD

title: Octal to Binary Encoder
description: Implement an octal to binary encoder. Converts an 8-bit one-hot octal input (0-7) to a 3-bit binary output. Only one of the 8 inputs should be active at a time. Output is the 3-bit binary representation of the active octal digit.
hint: out[2] = in[4] OR in[5] OR in[6] OR in[7]; similar for other bits

title: Hexadecimal to Binary Encoder
description: Implement a hexadecimal to binary encoder. Converts a 16-bit one-hot hexadecimal input (0-15) to a 4-bit binary output. Only one of the 16 inputs should be active at a time. Output is the 4-bit binary representation of the active hexadecimal digit (0-F).
hint: out[3] = in[8] OR in[9] OR ... OR in[15]; similar pattern for other bits

title: Binary to Gray Code Converter
description: Implement a 4-bit binary to Gray code converter. Gray code is a binary numeral system where two successive values differ in only one bit. Conversion formula: Gray[3] = Binary[3]; Gray[2] = Binary[3] XOR Binary[2]; Gray[1] = Binary[2] XOR Binary[1]; Gray[0] = Binary[1] XOR Binary[0].
hint: Gray MSB = Binary MSB; Gray other bits = XOR of adjacent binary bits

title: Gray Code to Binary Converter
description: Implement a 4-bit Gray code to binary converter. Reverse conversion from Gray code to binary. Conversion formula: Binary[3] = Gray[3]; Binary[2] = Gray[3] XOR Gray[2]; Binary[1] = Gray[3] XOR Gray[2] XOR Gray[1]; Binary[0] = Gray[3] XOR Gray[2] XOR Gray[1] XOR Gray[0].
hint: Binary bit i = XOR of Gray bits from MSB down to bit i

title: Even Parity Generator
description: Implement a 4-bit even parity generator. Even parity means the total number of 1s in the input plus the parity bit should be even. The parity bit p = XOR of all input bits. If XOR result is 0, parity bit is 0 (even number of 1s already); if XOR is 1, parity bit is 1 (makes total even).
hint: p = in[3] XOR in[2] XOR in[1] XOR in[0]

examples.explanation: 1 one in input, parity=1 makes total 2 (even)
2 ones in input, parity=0 keeps total 2 (even)

title: Odd Parity Generator
description: Implement a 4-bit odd parity generator. Odd parity means the total number of 1s in the input plus the parity bit should be odd. The parity bit p = NOT(XOR of all input bits). If XOR result is 0, parity bit is 1 (makes total odd); if XOR is 1, parity bit is 0 (keeps total odd).
hint: p = NOT(in[3] XOR in[2] XOR in[1] XOR in[0])

examples.explanation: 0 ones in input, parity=1 makes total 1 (odd)
1 one in input, parity=0 keeps total 1 (odd)

title: Even Parity Checker
description: Implement a 4-bit even parity checker. Checks if the received 4-bit data plus parity bit has even parity. error = 1 if parity error detected (total 1s is odd), error = 0 if correct (total 1s is even). Calculated as XOR of all 5 bits (4 data + 1 parity).
hint: error = in[3] XOR in[2] XOR in[1] XOR in[0] XOR p

title: Odd Parity Checker
description: Implement a 4-bit odd parity checker. Checks if the received 4-bit data plus parity bit has odd parity. error = 1 if parity error detected (total 1s is even), error = 0 if correct (total 1s is odd). Calculated as NOT(XOR of all 5 bits).
hint: error = NOT(in[3] XOR in[2] XOR in[1] XOR in[0] XOR p)

title: Binary to 7-Segment Display
description: Implement a BCD to 7-segment display decoder. Converts a 4-bit BCD input (0-9) to 7 outputs that control segments a-g of a common-cathode 7-segment display. Each output corresponds to one segment: a=MSB, g=LSB of output. Display digits 0-9 correctly, other inputs (10-15) should show blank (all segments off).
hint: Create case statement for bcd values 0-9 with hardcoded 7-bit patterns

title: Carry Look Ahead Adder
description: Implement a 4-bit carry look ahead adder (CLA). Unlike ripple carry adder, CLA computes all carry bits in parallel using generate (G) and propagate (P) signals. G[i]=A[i]&B[i], P[i]=A[i]|B[i]. Carry[i+1]=G[i]|(P[i]&Carry[i]). This is faster than ripple carry for wide adders.
hint: Pre-compute all carries: C1, C2, C3, Cout using G and P

title: BCD Adder
description: Implement a BCD (Binary Coded Decimal) adder that adds two 4-bit BCD digits (0-9) with carry-in and produces a 4-bit BCD sum and carry-out. BCD addition requires correction: if sum > 9 or carry from binary addition, add 6 (0110) to correct. Output should be valid BCD (0-9) with carry for next digit.
hint: First do binary addition, then check if result > 9, if yes add 6 and set carry

title: BCD to Excess-3 Converter
description: Implement a BCD to Excess-3 code converter. Excess-3 code is BCD + 3. Converts 4-bit BCD input (0-9) to 4-bit Excess-3 output. Invalid BCD inputs (10-15) can have don't care outputs. Excess-3 is self-complementing and useful in some arithmetic operations.
hint: Implement Boolean expressions: excess3[3] = bcd[3] OR (bcd[2] AND bcd[1]) OR (bcd[2] AND bcd[0])

title: Carry Save Adder
description: Implement a 4-bit carry save adder that adds three 4-bit numbers A, B, C. Carry save adder produces sum and carry vectors separately without propagating carry. Final addition of sum and carry vectors produces result. Used in multipliers and multi-operand addition.
hint: First stage: sum_temp[i] = a[i] XOR b[i] XOR c[i], carry_temp[i] = majority of a[i],b[i],c[i]. Second stage: Add sum_temp and {carry_temp[2:0], 1'b0}

title: Squares of 3-bit Numbers
description: Implement a circuit that computes the square of a 3-bit input number. Input is 3-bit binary (0-7), output is 6-bit square (0-49). Use combinational logic to implement the square function without multipliers.
hint: Derive Boolean expressions for each output bit: out[5]=in[2]&in[1], out[4]=(in[2]&~in[1])|(in[0]&in[2]), etc.

title: Tristate Buffer
description: Implement a tristate buffer with enable. When enable=1, output=input. When enable=0, output=high impedance (Z). Tristate buffers are used for bidirectional buses and shared lines where multiple devices can drive the same wire.
hint: Use conditional operator with 1'bz for high impedance

title: RS Latch using NOR Gates
description: Implement an RS latch using NOR gates. RS latch is the most basic memory element with two inputs: Set (S) and Reset (R), and two outputs: Q and Q_bar (complement). Truth table: S=0,R=0: hold; S=0,R=1: reset (Q=0); S=1,R=0: set (Q=1); S=1,R=1: invalid. Built with cross-coupled NOR gates.
hint: Cross-coupled NOR gates: q = ~(r | q_bar), q_bar = ~(s | q)

title: RS Latch using NAND Gates
description: Implement an RS latch using NAND gates. Similar to NOR latch but with active-low inputs. Inputs are typically S_bar and R_bar (active low). Truth table: S_bar=1,R_bar=1: hold; S_bar=1,R_bar=0: reset (Q=0); S_bar=0,R_bar=1: set (Q=1); S_bar=0,R_bar=0: invalid. Built with cross-coupled NAND gates.
hint: Cross-coupled NAND gates: q = ~(r_bar & q_bar), q_bar = ~(s_bar & q)

title: SR Flip-Flop
description: Implement a clocked SR flip-flop. SR flip-flop is a level-triggered sequential circuit with Set and Reset inputs controlled by a clock. When clock is high, behaves like RS latch. When clock is low, holds state. Avoids invalid state by ensuring S and R are never both 1 when clock is high.
hint: AND inputs with clock: q = ~(s & clk) NAND q_bar, q_bar = ~(r & clk) NAND q

examples.explanation: Clock low: Hold state regardless of inputs

title: JK Flip-Flop
description: Implement a positive-edge triggered JK flip-flop. JK flip-flop eliminates the invalid state of SR flip-flop. Truth table: J=0,K=0: hold; J=0,K=1: reset (Q=0); J=1,K=0: set (Q=1); J=1,K=1: toggle (Q=~Q). Changes occur only at positive clock edge.
hint: Use always @(posedge clk) with case({j,k})

examples.explanation: Positive edge with J=1,K=0 sets Q=1
Positive edge with J=1,K=1 toggles Q

title: D Flip-Flop
description: Implement a positive-edge triggered D flip-flop. D flip-flop stores the D input value at the positive clock edge. Q(t+1) = D(t). Simple and commonly used for data storage and synchronization. Changes only occur at positive clock edge.
hint: Simple: always @(posedge clk) q <= d;

examples.explanation: At positive edge, Q becomes D value (1)
Between clock edges, Q holds previous value

title: T Flip-Flop
description: Implement a positive-edge triggered T flip-flop with asynchronous reset. T flip-flop toggles its output when T=1 at clock edge, holds when T=0. Q(t+1) = Q(t) XOR T(t). Reset is active-low asynchronous (works regardless of clock).
hint: Use always @(posedge clk or negedge rst) with if(!rst) q<=0; else if(t) q<=~q;

examples.explanation: Toggle on clock edge when T=1

title: D Latch
description: Implement a level-sensitive D latch. D latch is transparent when enable=1 (Q follows D), and holds when enable=0 (Q maintains value). Unlike flip-flop, latch is level-sensitive rather than edge-triggered. Commonly used in latches and transparent registers.
hint: Use always @(*) if(en) q = d; (no else - holds automatically in latch)

title: Asynchronous Counter using T Flip-Flops
description: Implement a 4-bit asynchronous (ripple) counter using T flip-flops. Asynchronous counter connects Q output of each stage to clock of next stage. All T inputs are tied to 1. First flip-flop toggles on main clock, subsequent ones toggle on previous stage's output. Creates binary count sequence.
hint: Create 4 T flip-flops with T=1, chain clocks: clk->FF0, q[0]->FF1, q[1]->FF2, q[2]->FF3

title: Synchronous Up/Down Counter
description: Implement a 3-bit synchronous up/down counter with enable and reset. Synchronous means all flip-flops change on same clock edge. When en=1, count up; when en=0, count down. Reset clears counter to 0. Wraps around at limits (7 to 0 when up, 0 to 7 when down).
hint: Use always @(posedge clk) with if(rst) count<=0; else if(en) count<=count+1; else count<=count-1;

examples.explanation: Count up on clock edge when enabled
Count down on clock edge when disabled

title: Johnson Counter
description: Implement a 4-bit Johnson (twisted ring) counter. Johnson counter is a shift register with complement feedback. Pattern: 0000->1000->1100->1110->1111->0111->0011->0001->0000... Produces 8 unique states (2N states for N bits). Used for sequence generation.
hint: Use always @(posedge clk) with if(!rst) q<=0; else q<={q[2:0], ~q[3]};

title: Ring Counter
description: Implement a 4-bit ring counter using D flip-flops. Ring counter circulates a single 1 through the register. Pattern: 0001->0010->0100->1000->0001... Reset initializes to 0001. Used for control sequencing and timing generation.
hint: Use always @(posedge clk) with if(!rst) q<=4'b0001; else q<={q[2:0], q[3]};

title: Serial In Serial Out Shift Register
description: Implement a 4-bit Serial In Serial Out (SISO) shift register. Data shifts one bit per clock cycle: new bit enters at serial input, old bits shift left, last bit exits at serial output. Reset clears register to 0000. Basic building block for serial communication.
hint: Use always @(posedge clk) with if(!rst) q<=0; else q<={q[2:0], sin}; assign sout=q[3];

examples.explanation: Takes 4 clocks for input to reach output
First bit appears at output after 4 clocks

title: Serial In Parallel Out Shift Register
description: Implement a 4-bit Serial In Parallel Out (SIPO) shift register. Data shifts in serially one bit per clock, available in parallel after 4 clocks. Reset clears register to 0000. Used for serial-to-parallel conversion in communication interfaces.
hint: Use always @(posedge clk) with if(!rst) pout<=0; else pout<={pout[2:0], sin};

examples.explanation: Serial bits become parallel after 4 clocks

title: Parallel In Serial Out Shift Register
description: Implement a 4-bit Parallel In Serial Out (PISO) shift register with load control. When load=1, parallel data loads into register. When load=0, data shifts out serially each clock. Reset clears register. Used for parallel-to-serial conversion.
hint: Use always @(posedge clk) with if(!rst) q<=0; else if(ld) q<=pin; else q<={q[2:0], 1'b0}; assign sout=q[3];

title: Parallel In Parallel Out Shift Register
description: Implement a 4-bit Parallel In Parallel Out (PIPO) shift register with load control. When load=1, parallel data loads. When load=0, register shifts left each clock (LSB gets 0). Reset clears register. Parallel data always available at output.
hint: Use always @(posedge clk) with if(!rst) pout<=0; else if(ld) pout<=pin; else pout<={pout[2:0], 1'b0};

title: Master-Slave D Flip-Flop
description: Implement a master-slave D flip-flop. Two D latches in series: master latch transparent when clock=1, slave latch transparent when clock=0. Creates edge-triggered behavior from level-sensitive latches. Reset is asynchronous active-low.
hint: Create two D latches: master (clk), slave (~clk). master_out feeds slave_in. Reset clears both.

examples.explanation: Master captures at posedge, slave outputs at negedge

title: Sequence Detector (Mealy FSM)
description: Implement a Mealy finite state machine that detects sequence '101' in a serial bit stream. Mealy machine outputs depend on both current state and input. Output should be 1 when sequence detected, 0 otherwise. Overlapping sequences allowed (e.g., '10101' contains two '101's).
hint: Use 3 states. Output = (state==S2 && in==1). State transitions: S0->S1 if in=1, S1->S2 if in=0, S2->S1 if in=1, else appropriate transitions.

title: Sequence Detector (Moore FSM)
description: Implement a Moore finite state machine that detects sequence '101' in a serial bit stream. Moore machine outputs depend only on current state. Output should be 1 when in detecting state, 0 otherwise. Overlapping sequences allowed. Requires more states than Mealy for same sequence.
hint: Use 4 states. Output=1 only in state S3. State transitions: careful with overlapping cases from S3.

examples.explanation: Output 1 in state after receiving complete sequence
